opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the 2016 pilot was really a recommendation system at its core. We had trained models on years of sensor data from the data centers — temperatures, pump speeds, setpoints, power draw — and the system would predict what the energy efficiency would be under different configurations and then suggest actions. But a human operator still had to read those recommendations and go implement them by hand.

What we saw pretty quickly was that the bottleneck wasn't the intelligence of the model; it was the loop. The recommendations were good, and we were seeing roughly a 40% reduction in the energy used for cooling, but the operators are busy people. They're not going to sit there and adjust setpoints every few minutes, around the clock. So you'd get these bursts of improvement when someone was actively following the guidance, and then performance would drift back when they got pulled onto other things. The value was capped by human bandwidth.

So the obvious next question became: what if the system could act directly? Close the loop so it's continuously optimizing, every five minutes, 24/7, rather than whenever someone has time. That's where the real, sustained gains are.

Of course, that's a much harder problem, and not mainly for technical reasons. It's about trust and safety. You're talking about critical infrastructure where downtime is extremely costly. So we had to design it so the operators stayed in charge: multiple layers of constraints, the AI's actions verified against safety bounds before being applied, operators able to take control back at any moment, and the system defaulting to the existing, well-understood control logic if anything looked off. Earning that trust from the people on the floor was really the crux of it.

And once we had that working, it became pretty clear to me that this wasn't a Google-specific problem. Every industrial facility, from cooling plants to manufacturing, is run by these hand-tuned, rule-based systems that leave a lot of efficiency on the table. That realization is ultimately what led me to want to take this out to the broader industrial world.

r001.rationale: It says operators had to read the recommendations and implement them by hand.

r002.rationale: It cites roughly 40% lower cooling energy use from the pilot and describes the recommendations as good before explaining the move to continuous direct control.

r003.rationale: It explains that operators could not keep adjusting setpoints around the clock, so performance drifted when they were busy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the 2016 pilot was really the first big proof point. That was the DeepMind collaboration where we used neural networks to model the data center's cooling plant, and we got that roughly 40 percent reduction in cooling energy. But the important thing to understand about that first phase is that it was a recommendation system. The model would look at the state of the plant, predict what would happen under different setpoints, and then surface recommendations to the operators. A human would look at those, decide whether they made sense, and go implement them.

And that was the right way to start, because you're dealing with mission-critical infrastructure. If the cooling fails in a data center, servers overheat, and that's a very bad day for everyone. So you earn trust incrementally.

What we noticed, though, over the months of running it that way, was two things. First, the operators were accepting the recommendations the vast majority of the time. The system had basically become the thing making the decisions, with a human rubber-stamping it. Second, the value was capped by the human in the loop. A person can only act on a recommendation every so often. The plant is a dynamic system. Outside temperature changes, IT load changes, humidity changes, and the optimal configuration is shifting constantly. If you can only adjust a few times a day, you leave a lot on the table versus adjusting every five minutes.

So the natural question became: what would it take for the AI to actually drive the plant itself? And that reframes everything. It's no longer "is this a good prediction," it's "is this a safe action." We spent a huge amount of effort on the safety layer. The model would propose an action, and then it would go through a verification system that checked it against hard constraints the operators had defined. If anything looked off, control fell back to the existing rule-based systems. The operators always had a big red button, essentially.

And what surprised me was how much more the system could do once it was in the loop directly. It found strategies the human team hadn't considered, because it could exploit interactions between pieces of equipment that happen on timescales people don't operate on. That's really when I became convinced that direct control, done carefully, was the path. You keep humans setting the objectives and the guardrails, but you let the system handle the moment-to-moment decisions, because that's where it's actually better than we are.

r001.rationale: It says the pilot surfaced recommendations that a human reviewed, judged, and implemented.

r002.rationale: It cites a roughly 40 percent reduction in cooling energy from the pilot as a proof point.

r003.rationale: It explains that operators could act only every so often, limiting adjustments to a few times a day while conditions changed constantly, motivating direct control.

astra-6.text:
The 2016 pilot showed that AI could make useful recommendations for running a data center more efficiently. But there was still a person in the loop who had to look at those recommendations and translate them into actions. That made us ask: if the system can figure out what to do, could it also carry out those actions safely?

That’s a bigger step than it might sound. Giving advice and being responsible for control are very different things. You need constraints on what the system can do, checks before an action is taken, and a way for operators to take over. So I saw direct control as the next step because it could close that gap between a good recommendation and an actual improvement, while making safety central to the design.

r001.rationale: It says a person had to review the AI’s recommendations and translate them into actions.

r002.rationale: It describes recommendations for greater efficiency but does not identify demonstrated energy savings.

r003.rationale: It notes that a person had to review and act on recommendations, but does not identify the burden of repeatedly doing so as a motivation for automation.

sol-6.1.text:
The 2016 pilot showed us that AI could make useful recommendations about how to run the cooling system more efficiently. But there was still a person in the loop who had to look at those recommendations, decide what to do, and implement them.

That raised a pretty natural question: if the system can figure out what actions to take, could it also take those actions directly? Cooling conditions change continuously, and having an operator translate recommendations into control changes limits how quickly you can respond. It also puts more work on the operator.

The next step was to close that loop, but with safety as the central design constraint. You don’t just give a model unrestricted control of a data center. You need limits on what it can do, checks on its decisions, and a way to hand control back when it’s uncertain. So I saw direct control as the next step in turning a promising recommendation system into something that could reliably operate in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says a person had to review the AI’s recommendations, decide what to do, and implement the changes.

r002.rationale: It says the pilot produced useful efficiency recommendations, but does not identify demonstrated energy savings as evidence for moving to direct control.

r003.rationale: It describes operators repeatedly translating recommendations into control changes as conditions change, which slows response and adds work, motivating closing the loop.
